{{Short description|Structure over a vocabulary defined solely by syntactical properties}}
In [[first-order logic]], a '''Herbrand structure''' <math>S</math> is a [[Structure (mathematical logic)|structure]] over a [[Signature (logic)#Other conventions|vocabulary]] <math>\sigma</math> (also sometimes called a ''signature'') that is defined solely by the syntactical properties of  <math>\sigma</math>. The idea is to take the symbol strings of [[Term (logic)|terms]] as their values, e.g. the denotation of a constant symbol <math>c</math> is just "<math>c</math>" (the symbol). It is named after [[Jacques Herbrand]].

Herbrand structures play an important role in the foundations of [[logic programming]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://logic.stanford.edu/herbrand/herbrand.html|title=Herbrand Semantics|access-date=2017-04-05|archive-date=2017-05-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170523123025/http://logic.stanford.edu/herbrand/herbrand.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Herbrand universe==
===Definition===

The ''Herbrand universe'' serves as the universe in a ''Herbrand structure''.
{{olist
|<div> The ''Herbrand universe'' of a first-order language <math>L^\sigma</math>, is the set of all [[ground term]]s of <math>L^\sigma</math>. If the language has no constants, then the language is extended by adding an arbitrary new constant.

* The Herbrand universe is [[countably infinite]] if <math>\sigma</math> is [[countable]] and a function symbol of [[arity]] greater than 0 exists. 
* In the context of first-order languages we also speak simply of the ''Herbrand universe'' of the vocabulary <math>\sigma</math>.
</div>
|<div> The ''Herbrand universe'' of a [[Closed formula (mathematical logic)|closed formula]] in [[Skolem normal form]] <math>F</math> is the set of all terms without variables that can be constructed using the function symbols and constants of <math>F</math>. If <math>F</math> has no constants, then <math>F</math> is extended by adding an arbitrary new constant.

* This second definition is important in the context of [[Resolution (logic)|computational resolution]].
</div>
}}

===Example===

Let <math>L^\sigma</math>, be a first-order language with the vocabulary 
* constant symbols: <math>c</math>
* function symbols: <math>f(\cdot), \, g(\cdot)</math>
then the Herbrand universe <math>H</math> of <math>L^\sigma</math> (or of <math>\sigma</math>) is

<math> H = \{ c, f(c), g(c), f(f(c)), f(g(c)), g(f(c)), g(g(c)), \dots\} </math>

The [[First-order logic#Non-logical symbols|relation symbols]] are not relevant for a Herbrand universe since formulas involving only relations do not correspond to elements of the universe.<ref>

Formulas consisting only of relations <math>R</math> evaluated at a set of constants or variables correspond to subsets of finite powers of the universe <math>H^n</math> where <math>n</math> is the arity of <math>R</math>.

</ref>

==Herbrand structure==

A ''Herbrand structure'' interprets terms on top of a ''Herbrand universe''.

===Definition===

Let <math>S</math> be a [[Structure (mathematical logic)|structure]], with vocabulary <math>\sigma</math> and universe <math>U</math>. Let <math>W</math> be the set of all terms over <math>\sigma</math> and <math>W_0</math> be the subset of all variable-free terms. <math>S</math> is said to be a ''Herbrand structure'' iff

# <math>U = W_0</math>
# <math>f^S(t_1,\dots,t_n) = f(t_1,\dots,t_n)</math> for every <math>n</math>-ary function symbol <math>f \in \sigma</math> and <math>t_1,\dots,t_n \in W_0</math>
# <math>c^S = c</math> for every constant <math>c</math> in <math>\sigma</math>

===Remarks===

# <math>U</math> is the Herbrand universe of <math>\sigma</math>.
# A Herbrand structure that is a [[model (logic)|model]] of a [[theory (logic)|theory]] <math>T</math> is called a ''Herbrand model'' of <math>T</math>.

===Examples===

For a constant symbol <math>c</math> and a unary function symbol <math>f(\,\cdot\,)</math> we have the following interpretation:

* <math>U = \{c, fc, ffc, fffc, \dots\} </math>
* <math>fc \mapsto fc, ffc \mapsto ffc, \dots</math>
* <math>c \mapsto c</math>

==Herbrand base==
In addition to the universe, defined in {{sectionlink||Herbrand universe}}, and the term denotations, defined in {{sectionlink||Herbrand structure}}, the ''Herbrand base'' completes the interpretation by denoting the relation symbols.

===Definition===

A ''Herbrand base'' <math>\mathcal B_H</math> for a Herbrand structure is the set of all atomic formulas whose argument terms are elements of the Herbrand universe.

===Examples===

For a binary relation symbol <math>R</math>, we get with the terms from above:

: <math>\mathcal B_H = \{R(c,c), R(fc,c), R(c,fc), R(fc,fc), R(ffc,c), \dots\} </math>
